title: Binary Tree Vertical Order Traversal
statement:
You are given `root`, the root of a binary tree. Give every node a column number: the root is in column `0`, a left child is one column to the left of its parent (column minus 1), and a right child is one column to the right (column plus 1).

Return the node values grouped by column, with the groups ordered from the leftmost column to the rightmost one. Inside a group, values are listed from the top of the tree downward (smaller depth first). When two nodes share both a column and a depth, the one that comes first when that depth is read from left to right is listed first.

Return an empty list when the tree has no nodes.
constraints: The tree has between 0 and 100 nodes.
notes:
## Intuition

A brute-force idea walks the tree in any order, records each node's column and depth, and sorts by column, then depth, then left-to-right position. A breadth-first sweep removes the need for the depth and position keys: it reaches nodes level by level, and inside a level from left to right, which is exactly the order wanted inside each column. So it is enough to carry each node's column through the queue and append its value to that column's list in a hash map.

The columns that appear always form an unbroken range (a node in column 3 has ancestors in columns 2, 1 and 0), so tracking the smallest and largest column replaces sorting the map's keys.

## Approach

1. Return `[]` for an empty tree.
2. Put `[root, 0]` in `queue`; `head` marks the next pair to process.
3. Take the pair `[node, col]` at `head`, append `node.val` to `columns.get(col)` (creating the list if needed), and widen `minCol`/`maxCol`.
4. Queue the left child with `col - 1`, then the right child with `col + 1`.
5. When the queue is drained, collect the lists from `minCol` to `maxCol` into `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

Tree `[3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7]`. The queue gives, in order: `3` at column 0, `9` at -1, `20` at 1, `15` at 0 (left child of 20) and `7` at 2. So `columns` becomes `{0: [3, 15], -1: [9], 1: [20], 2: [7]}` with `minCol = -1` and `maxCol = 2`. Reading columns -1 to 2 returns `[[9], [3, 15], [20], [7]]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each node enters and leaves the queue once, and building `result` touches each column once.
- Space: O(n): the queue and the column lists together hold every node at most once each.

## Pitfalls

- A plain depth-first walk lists a deep node before a shallower one in the same column. In example 3 it would give column 0 as `[1, 10, 6, 9]` instead of `[1, 10, 9, 6]`.
- Iterating the `Map` directly yields columns in insertion order, not from left to right; walk from `minCol` to `maxCol`.
- Queue the left child before the right child so ties at the same depth stay in left-to-right order.
- Handle an empty `root` before reading `root.val`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `columns` | map from column number to the values found in it, in visit order |
| `minCol`, `maxCol` | leftmost and rightmost columns seen |
| `queue` | pairs `[node, col]` waiting to be visited, in breadth-first order |
| `head` | index of the next pair in `queue` |
| `node`, `col` | the node being visited and its column |
| `result` | the column lists from left to right |
